It's also hard to track — it could be a bad batch, an end-product inconsistency, or material you knew you shouldn't have run through but did anyway to make it work.

Bryan Fields: You spend so much money to acquire that customer the first time. They come back a second and third time, then have a bad experience but stay loyal for a bit, then eventually move to another brand — and it's disheartening because you don't see those lost sales clearly.

Brian Adams: Right, and we're not vertically integrated like a lot of companies here in Massachusetts. If you had retail, you might get that feedback much quicker and adjust faster. We have to rely on our retail partners and on consumers reaching out, so our feedback loop is much slower. I always want to hear feedback as soon as possible so we can sift through it and make an adjustment. But sometimes it's tough — if you spent well into six figures on a big batch of hardware you were confident in and it goes south, how do you rectify that? We've had to discard a lot of hardware because we didn't want to ruin our brand's reputation. That comes down to whether the hardware manufacturer takes ownership of their responsibility and what they'll do to support us as a partner. We've had to move on from partners when, in our opinion, they didn't do what was right to remedy the situation.

Bryan Fields: Have you thought about expanding the brand into other categories, or do you want to lock in on a few?

Brian Adams: Nimbus really just wants to be known for high-quality smokable cannabis. We want to play in all the smokable categories and be at the top of the pile in all of them. Even though people hate on distillate, it's the king and it's where the sales are, so it's going to be a cheaper product, but we want to make sure it's the best distillate vape in the category. We want the best live resin in the category, the best pre-rolls, some of the best flower. All those smokable categories are where we want to play, at a very high level, respected for quality and value.

Bryan Fields: How do you transfer that metric of quality internally, since it can be preference-driven? How do you define quality and set the standard to meet it?

Brian Adams: That's an ongoing battle we're always chasing. We get feedback from the market, and especially when launching something new we try to survey outside of our company as much as possible so we can make adjustments or price things accordingly based on the feedback. A lot of people in cannabis race to get something out on the market — we've done it many times, getting excited to show something new without getting that consumer feedback and iteration to reach the highest level product. That's something we're focusing on this year and going forward — compiling more true market feedback so we're making products people really want, even if it's not our personal favorite. We just want to make sure it's the highest level of quality possible in that category.

Bryan Fields: Right, so when someone sees the Nimbus brand, they know exactly what to expect — versus walking in looking for a value-minus brand where they just want to buy something cheap.

Brian Adams: Exactly. We want people to have a good experience they can write home about and come back to purchase again. I'm not going to say we hit that every single time — we're not perfect — but we're striving to be, and we're going to keep chipping away, lowering that swing so the level of quality gets tighter as we get better. That comes from innovation and a dedicated team, and we just have to keep making sure every batch is at the highest possible standard.

Bryan Fields: And that consistency standpoint requires understanding the limitations of your system, having the right operator, the nuances, the flexible dynamics — that's where extraction people don't understand how stacked the variables become, and to do it at a high standard you have to stack all of those on top of each other for a long period of time.

Brian Adams: Oh yeah, it's a balancing act. A lot of people go into a dispensary and buy a product without thinking about what's behind the scenes. There's a lot of hard work beyond just producing the product — amazing cultivation partners keeping us well provided with good quality material, a great sales team working with retail partners to make sure it's placed correctly, and a marketing team making sure it's positioned correctly. It's a lot of moving parts that go into that one little vape cart you buy at the dispensary.

Bryan Fields: When you first got started with processing at Nimbus, did you imagine it would involve this many layers and variables?

Brian Adams: I had somewhat of an understanding because before starting this I worked for Wana, and I got a taste of it there — this is a crazy industry with a lot of moving parts, and one company does a lot to produce a product. It's not like calling a factory in China, telling them what you want, and they make it and send it to you — definitely not that simple. I had a little understanding coming in, but taking it to the next level of contract manufacturing, doing it for other people, on top of extraction and not just making edibles like Wana does — there's more nuance and moving parts that make it interesting, but that's also part of the fun.

Bryan Fields: Right — small batch is one problem, and as you scale up you hit new problems, hardware being one, consistent products being another. Early on you succeed at small scale, then midscale, and as you accelerate further there are new challenges right around the corner that you didn't see coming.

Brian Adams: Yeah, it keeps me on my toes, that's for sure.

Bryan Fields: Why does clean BHO always win?

Brian Adams: I'm probably going to get a lot of flack for this one. I'm not going to hate on the rosin people or the solventless community — I have a lot of respect for them, and it's a product I thoroughly enjoy — but when it comes to a true clean concentrate, if you're making hydrocarbon BHO dabs the correct way, with the proper equipment, proper SOPs, people who give a damn, and good material going in — the same level of quality that a solventless hash maker would use going into a hydrocarbon system — it's hard to argue that it's not the cleanest concentrate out there, if it's done right. The cannabinoids, the aromas, the terpenes, everything the plant has to offer — that's BHO. It's literally the complete essence of the plant, whereas solventless has other compounds in the mix that make it not necessarily the cleanest. There's also a wider variability in quality when producing solventless, even at a super high level — an innate mixture of quality based on the starting material — where with hydrocarbon you can dial your process in and tighten that scale of quality to be more consistent and get an overall cleaner smoke.

Bryan Fields: How do we get consumers who walk in to understand those nuanced differences when making a selection?

Brian Adams: A lot of time and effort. I think we all have to collectively put effort into educating the consumer — we're still such a baby industry in the grand scheme of things. I don't knock people who walk in, see BHO, and ask what that is — when you hear "butane honey oil," you hear "butane" and think, wait, that's the stuff in my lighter, I shouldn't be ingesting that. In reality, when made correctly, all the butane is gone — it was just the medium to making the concentrate. When you hear solventless and think it's just washed in water with heat and pressure, I get how that sounds less harmful, but in reality that product can be more bio-inclusive, with waxes, fats, and other things getting into your body. If you're trying to smoke concentrates, I think you're trying to be cleaner, and rosin is a step in the right direction, but there are other compounds in there that come into play.

Bryan Fields: It's a difficult balance — people make split-second decisions and think they're selecting one product when in reality they might really want the BHO product but didn't recognize the nuance differences.

Brian Adams: Right, understanding how it's made — that's one thing we're doing now, this first quarter and going forward. We're trying to put out more behind-the-scenes content, more QR codes on our packaging that go to videos so people can scan quickly and get an understanding of how we do things and how products are produced, because a lot of people have no idea. And a lot of people just don't care to know either — they want to get their product, get stoned, and move on with their day, which I understand. But how do we get in front of those people and give them correct information? There's also a lot of BS information and other agendas being pushed that make it challenging.

Bryan Fields: Especially in the concentrate category, where the word "quality" gets framed in different ways, and illustrating that to consumers gets layered with challenges when the person down the street is doing it differently.

Bryan Fields: So, Massachusetts rolling back adult use — on a scale of 1 to 10, how real is that outcome today versus just political noise?

Brian Adams: I think it's a very real possibility. I'd say a seven, honestly, if I had to put a number on it. It could be more of a flip of a coin, but even the fact that it feels like a flip of a coin is a huge problem, something we've got to be paying attention to.

Bryan Fields: Why do you think this is coming up now?

Brian Adams: I don't know why it's coming up now, to be honest. The Massachusetts recreational cannabis scene has had a lot of negative news the past couple of years, and maybe the opposition feels that because there's so much negative news, now is the time to strike, because they can build on that. There's been a lot of unfortunate negative news around the cannabis sector generally, with stuff being sold in convenience stores and kids getting their hands on hemp products that are much more psychoactive than a typical product. Not that kids should be getting their hands on THC products at all, but they've had much easier access. Unfortunately people like us trying to do it the right way, going through a tight regulatory system and a crazy licensing process, get lumped in with that, and I think they see this as an opportunity to attack. They just don't want cannabis or any mind-altering substances in our society. In my opinion, it should be the individual's choice what they do with their body and life, as long as they're not bothering others. It comes down to a philosophical understanding of how you want society to be run. Unfortunately these people are really well-funded, with big pockets, and they're very calculated — they're choosing a non-presidential, midterm election year, when fewer people show up, typically an older crowd. You can see the playbook.

Bryan Fields: That's got to be scary — you spend your days figuring out how to make a consistent product and grow the business, and now you're getting a call saying, by the way, they're talking about a rollback. When you shared that with me I was shocked — I hadn't heard about it, and I can only imagine you thinking, is this real?

Brian Adams: Yeah, and what was crazy is we'd heard early noise that they were putting together a ballot campaign initiative to push forward in Massachusetts, and we thought, these people are trying, but there's no chance. We brushed it off for a while, and then boom, all of a sudden they got all the signatures they needed to get it on the ballot, and we thought, oh damn, these people are serious. Then hearing reports of what they were even paying signature gatherers — a lot of money — and looking at these campaigns' balance sheets, what they've got in the bank, these people are well-funded and ready to push. They're doing it in Maine, in Arizona, and now here, prepared to spend big to try to put the cap back in the bag. It's scary, and it's something the industry has to get behind — we've got to put industry BS aside and come together as a cohesive industry to fight this common enemy, so we're even able to keep selling products and building on what a lot of hardworking people have built.

Bryan Fields: What's a signal that would make you feel like this is getting worse?

Brian Adams: They're going to put ads out — I'm curious about their messaging. I think we'll start to see ads pretty soon; the election cycle is coming up quicker than we think, the Olympics are coming up, there's a lot of general viewership, and they'll take advantage of that airtime. I want to see what the messaging is and how mainstream media picks it up, because midterm elections typically bring out an older demographic that's still tied to traditional media, so how traditional media handles the messaging will be a telltale sign.

Bryan Fields: A lot of that generation grew up with "weed is a gateway drug," "devil's lettuce" messaging. I'd imagine they'll go after "the children are using it," which statistically has been disproven, and maybe addiction rates and medical error. Does Schedule III help alleviate any of those concerns, or is it an independent thing?

Brian Adams: I don't know — the Schedule III move makes you wonder if it plays into the hands of pharma, and whether pharma is potentially behind some of this opposition. I have no idea, but it seems strange these things are happening around the same time. Are they correlated? Going to Schedule III, maybe more FDA regulation, that plays right into pharma's existing infrastructure. Is this playing into their hands, or complete coincidence? Could be a total coincidence and the people at SAM just happen to have Schedule III happen in the same time frame. We'll see.

Bryan Fields: It's definitely odd. Are there coincidences? Feels like there's never any coincidences, but it's hard to know.

Brian Adams: Yeah, and unfortunately in Massachusetts the negative news around the CCC and how the state has handled the recreational rollout hasn't gone as smoothly as we all hoped.

Bryan Fields: It's better than some other states.

Brian Adams: Yeah, but still a lot of big fumbles. I'd say somewhere in the middle of the road in my analysis — better than some, not as good as others — but a lot of classic old-school Massachusetts politics that go down and don't help our narrative.

Bryan Fields: In this grading scheme, middle of the pack should be curved up, because there are states where you'd say "yikes" — if they just did the opposite of everything they've done, they'd do way better, instead of expensive politicians lobbying for bad decisions time after time.

Brian Adams: Yeah, it's wild. I can't believe we're even here talking about this — I never thought they'd want to put it completely back in the bag. But if you look back at the history of alcohol, there were perils too — here in Massachusetts there was the blue law era, they got rid of happy hour, and people fought it along the way. My real hope is this brings the industry closer together, that we team up to combat the poor messaging, and ultimately prevail. We all have to be on the same page, with the same messaging, and come together as one community to fight for what we think is right.

Bryan Fields: At this stage we can never say never, but it seems unlikely — Massachusetts is a major state, they do serious numbers, employ a lot of jobs, and I hope they use sensible logic making these decisions. But you're right, there's a fear-based approach from an older generation who thinks it's the same weed they smoked in their college dorm room, and it's not — maybe that needs generational dialogue, and maybe that means recognizing we can all be adults and make our own choices.

Brian Adams: Exactly, that's what we've got to push for — it's just freedom. This is America. You should have the ability to be free and make your own choices as long as you're not harming your neighbor. I hope other people share that sentiment, and if we look to help ourselves while protecting our neighbor, we'd all be in a better place.

Bryan Fields: 100%. Last question — what question do you wish more people asked you?

Brian Adams: That's a good one. I wish people asked more about how we produce things. I think that gets lost in "how much is the product, what can I get it for, that's that." A lot of people don't get curious about how or why it's produced. I wish people asked more about how we came to the products we've put out and what the story behind that is — I'd love for people to ask more about the journey.

Bryan Fields: I think that's great, and it's smart to use the QR codes and behind-the-scenes videos — shout out to Jack and all those guys, because I think you're doing a really good job, and I think those small details will help separate the brand as people recognize the nuance, the love and affection that goes into making these products, and why they can command consistent quality on a regular basis. So Brian, for our listeners who want to get in touch and buy your products, where can they find you?

Brian Adams: Please follow us on Instagram at Nimbus CC. You can reach out to us on our website at nimbuscannabisco.com. If you're in Massachusetts, keep your eyes out — many dispensaries carry our products, and we're slowly but surely growing the brand down in New Jersey. We appreciate any feedback, we welcome it, we want to hear it — we're always trying to improve and be better. We appreciate the cannabis community, and we hope to continue improving here in 2026.

Bryan Fields: Thanks for taking the time, this was a lot of fun.

Brian Adams: Thanks, man.
summary: In this episode, Brian Adams of Nimbus discusses why rigid, one-size-fits-all extraction SOPs fail in practice, how his team learned to adjust processes based on material variability, and why proactively defining an end goal — yield versus flavor and color — beats reactive downstream fixes. The conversation also covers the hidden importance and inconsistency risks of vape hardware, the economics of when a brand should outsource extraction rather than run it in-house, why well-made BHO can rival or beat solventless concentrates on purity, and the industry's fight against a looming ballot initiative to roll back adult-use cannabis in Massachusetts.
takeaways: Identical SOPs don't guarantee identical extraction results because material variability, operator skill, and equipment consistency all significantly affect outcomes.
Top extraction teams empower operators to make real-time adjustments rather than rigidly following a fixed process, which requires significant coaching and development over time.
Defining the end goal (max yield vs. max color/flavor) before running an extraction is more effective than extracting first and deciding what to do with the result afterward.

Companies without equipment capable of maintaining consistent temperature/conditions throughout a run are often at the mercy of variable results and should consider outsourcing to specialists instead.
Vape hardware is often the hidden cause of consumer complaints even when the oil itself is high quality, and hardware manufacturers can become inconsistent once scaled to mass production.
One bad product experience can permanently lose a loyal customer, and most dissatisfied consumers never voice complaints — they simply stop buying, making the problem hard to track.
Well-made hydrocarbon (BHO) concentrate can be argued to be cleaner and more consistent than solventless products, which carry more variability tied to starting material quality.

A well-funded ballot initiative poses a real (roughly 7-out-of-10 likelihood, per the guest) risk of rolling back adult-use cannabis in Massachusetts, and the guest urges the industry to unite against it.

faq.question: Why doesn't following the same extraction SOP guarantee consistent results?
faq.answer: Because results are driven heavily by the operator and the incoming material, not just the process itself; even similar lots of material from the same source can behave differently, so extraction teams need to make on-the-fly adjustments rather than rigidly following one fixed procedure.

faq.question: When does it make more financial sense for a cannabis brand to outsource extraction rather than run it in-house?
faq.answer: When a company can't achieve enough volume or consistent quality with its own equipment, the cost structure often doesn't make sense; outsourcing to a specialized processor with better equipment and cost efficiency can be more economical than continuing to invest in an underperforming in-house program.

faq.question: Why is vape hardware so important to the customer experience, even though the oil is the main product?
faq.answer: Hardware acts like the 'producer' delivering the oil's experience to the consumer — even great oil can perform poorly, clog, or fail to vaporize properly if the hardware is inconsistent, especially once production scales to hundreds of thousands of units.

faq.question: Is BHO (butane hash oil) cleaner than solventless concentrates like rosin?
faq.answer: According to extraction expert Brian Adams, when made correctly with proper equipment, SOPs, and quality material, hydrocarbon BHO can be the cleanest form of concentrate, preserving the plant's cannabinoids and terpenes without the waxes and fats sometimes present in solventless products, and offers more consistent quality control than solventless extraction.

faq.question: How real is the risk that Massachusetts could roll back adult-use cannabis?
faq.answer: Guest Brian Adams rated the possibility at around a 7 out of 10, noting that a well-funded, organized ballot campaign has already gathered enough signatures to get a rollback measure on the ballot, timed strategically for a lower-turnout midterm election year.

faq.question: Why do some cannabis consumers stop buying a product after one bad experience?
faq.answer: Cannabis consumers tend to be highly fickle; most people who have a subpar experience don't complain, they simply switch brands, making it hard for companies to track the true scope of dissatisfaction and lost repeat customers.

faq.question: What role might Schedule III rescheduling play in the push to roll back state cannabis programs?
faq.answer: The guest speculates, without certainty, that the timing of Schedule III rescheduling alongside opposition ballot campaigns is curious, raising the question of whether pharmaceutical industry interests could be indirectly connected to anti-cannabis efforts, though he stresses this is speculation, not confirmed fact.
